statement: For an irreducible finite-type k-scheme X and any k-morphism X→P^r, its section over the generic point of the dual space is empty or irreducible; if nonempty it dominates X. This is ordinary, not geometric, irreducibility.
computation: Proof: the total incidence over X is irreducible. Localizing its coordinate rings at the nonzero functions of the dual base gives an empty scheme or an irreducible generic fiber, whose generic point is also generic in the incidence and hence maps to the generic point of X.
fate: The incidence projective-bundle argument proves this exact statement. Stacks0G4C separately treats the stronger geometric version, whose image-dimension hypothesis must not be omitted.

statement: The image in P^r of the generic hyperplane consists exactly of the nonclosed points. For constructible Z⊂X of finite type over k, its generic section is empty iff f(Z) is finite.
computation: Proof: a closed point has finite residue extension, so its incidence image is a proper hyperplane locus. The closure of a nonclosed point has positive dimension; if a hyperplane missed it, that closure would be both affine and proper, hence finite. A constructible subset of a finite-type Jacobson space consisting only of closed points is finite.
fate: The exact visibility statement follows from projective incidence and the fact that a positive-dimensional projective closed subset meets every hyperplane. Stacks0G4C uses the same generic-section setup.

statement: Under the component-image and finite-image-deletion hypotheses of3.3, with X proper over an algebraically closed field, every hyperplane section is connected, including excess-dimensional sections.
computation: Proof: for an integral component apply Stein factorization to proper incidence. Its generic fiber is geometrically connected. The reduced finite factor is generically purely inseparable over the normal projective dual space; on a normal affine base each integral element has a p-power in the base, so this finite factor is universally injective and has connected fibers (birational in characteristic0). For reducible X, form the finite graph of components joined when their intersection has positive-dimensional image. The deletion hypothesis makes this graph connected. Such an intersection has proper positive-dimensional image, which meets every hyperplane. Each component section is connected, so their union is connected.
fate: For an integral source, EGA III1 Corollary4.3.7 and Remark4.3.8, printed133, gives the proper connectedness-specialization step over the normal dual projective space. Martinelli–Naranjo–Pirola Theorem1.1 supplies the irreducible projective case in any characteristic. The manuscript’s reducible case additionally uses its finite-image-deletion hypothesis; it is not a verbatim case of either cited theorem.

statement: For smooth geometrically irreducible immersed X⊂P^r with nonempty conormal incidence, generic unramifiedness of the conormal projection is equivalent to a finite separable function-field extension and to a nonsupersingular tangency. Under these hypotheses the dual is a hypersurface and the conormal map is birational; over the smooth dual it is an open immersion, and an isomorphism if X is proper.
computation: Targeted proof check: the differential image at (x,H) identifies the hyperplane in the dual tangent space determined by x; two points over a smooth dual point must therefore coincide. Properness upgrades the open immersion to an isomorphism there.
fate: The exact separable-duality argument is developed in SGA7II XVII§3. Nonempty incidence and immersion are essential; neither a linear full-dimensional X nor arbitrary unramified multiple covers can be silently included in the birational statement.

statement: For a regular rank2 section defining an axis T, the incidence pencil is Bl_T X. A generic pencil avoids a closed bad locus of codimension≥2. The deleted10.3 suggests the higher-rank regular-section/Rees-algebra version but leaves its proof to be supplied.
computation: Proof: in a regular two-generator ideal(a,b), its Rees algebra is A[U,V]/(bU−aV), giving exactly the pencil incidence. Basis changes preserve the Koszul regularity in the local regular-immersion setting. The counterexample to replacing a closed bad locus by an arbitrary constructible one is a line with its intersection point with the chosen pencil-line removed.
fate: The regular-ideal Rees construction is standard; Stacks01OF gives the blow-up universal property. SGA7II XVII2 defines the pencil blow-up and its ordinary singular fibers. A single line avoiding a nonclosed constructible subset does not prove the codimension bound for its closure.

statement: For a quasi-coherent E on S, the rank-n locally free quotient functor is represented by Grass_n(E), compatible with base change, with its Plücker morphism toP(∧^nE). For finite-rank locally free E, rank r, the standard charts are affine spaces of dimension n(r−n), and Grass_n(E) is smooth and projective/S.

statement: The chart of rank-n quotients restricting to an isomorphism on E′ is identified canonically with the vector bundle after a basis decomposition of E. The text deletes “sommes directes” in favor of exact sequences but retains the preceding basis choice. Extending “canonical” to an arbitrary exact sequence is a stronger reading, not forced by that context.
computation: Proof: two retractions E→E′ differ by a map E″→E′, and retractions exist locally for a locally split sequence. A global retraction is equivalent to a splitting. A nonzero extension of O by O on a genus1 curve is locally split and has finite locally free terms, but no global retraction because its class in Ext¹(O,O)=H¹(O) is nonzero. Its retraction torsor therefore has no global zero section. This refutes only the unrestricted canonical-trivialization reading. The sequence0→2Z→Z→Z/2→0 has no retraction even after faithfully flat base change, illustrating the necessity of local splitting for the torsor formulation.
fate: The chosen-basis chart is valid. For a locally split exact sequence with finite locally free E′ and E″, the chart is the torsor of retractions under Hom(E″,E′); choosing a splitting trivializes it. A nonsplit extension shows that a choice-free global vector-bundle identification is false. Without local splitting even the torsor assertion can fail. Stacks089R uses the valid split coordinate charts. The unresolved issue is the scope of the source’s “une telle suite exacte,” not the standard chart theorem.

statement: An elementary fibration is an open in a smooth projective family of geometrically connected curves with nonempty finite étale boundary. Over an infinite perfect field, a smooth point on a geometrically irreducible finite-type scheme has a basis of opens admitting towers of elementary fibrations.
computation: Targeted proof check: Artin XI3.3 was read with its algebraically closed-field hypothesis. Schmidt–Stix Lemma6.3 and its full proof were read: the good choices over a geometric point form a nonempty open in the Grassmannian; intersect its finitely many Galois conjugates and use rationality of the Grassmannian over the infinite field. Induction gives the tower. Attribution of the original construction remains Artin.
fate: The text credits M.Artin. Original SGA4III XI3.1 and3.3, printed68–72, gives the definition and the algebraically closed-field neighborhood theorem at a rational point. Schmidt–Stix2016 Lemma6.3 explicitly proves the infinite-perfect-field extension, including nonrational points, by an open Grassmannian condition and finite Galois conjugates. The source proof has local-choice gaps, so these later exact results are not a certificate of each sentence here.

statement: For a complex poly-elementary neighborhood of dimension n, the analytic space is a K(pi,1); its fundamental group is built by successive extensions by finitely generated free groups, and its universal cover is homeomorphic toC^n. This is a topological, not biholomorphic, assertion.
computation: Proof: compactify each curve fibration with finite étale boundary. Ehresmann’s theorem for the compact pair gives a locally trivial bundle of punctured surfaces. Pull to the universal cover of the base; the bundle over its contractible R^(2n−2) base is trivial, and then take the contractible surface cover R². The homotopy exact sequence gives the free-group extension and vanishing higher homotopy.
fate: SGA4III XI’s comparison argument uses elementary neighborhoods and their topological fibration structure. A punctured compact complex curve has contractible universal cover; the tower gives asphericity. The stronger homeomorphism statement uses triviality of a smooth bundle over a contractible base, not uniformization in several variables.

statement: For an m-dimensional projective X with a finite map toP^r, a generic linear projection avoiding the image gives a finite surjection X→P^m; the quasi-finite version applies on the corresponding open and is dominant.

statement: For E finite locally free of rank at least2 everywhere, the relative effective degree-n divisors in P(E), n≥0, are represented by P((Sym^n E)^vee). Scan107 expressly corrects scan5, which used Sym^n(E^vee). A divisor is a fiberwise regular section of p*M(n), equivalently a sub-line-bundle M^−1 of Sym^n E. The separate cancelled restatement on scan112 omits the dual on Sym^n E and does not repeat the rank-at-least2 hypothesis; it is retained as another source occurrence, not silently normalized. The formula is not extended to rank1: then P(E)=S, the relative Cartier divisor is empty, and the degree labels do not distinguish different divisors.
computation: Proof: every nonzero homogeneous polynomial over a field is a nonzerodivisor in its polynomial ring. Fiberwise nonzero sections therefore give relative Cartier divisors. A locally split line inclusion in Sym^n E dualizes to a rank-one quotient of (Sym^n E)^vee, exactly the functor represented by the stated projective bundle.
fate: The relative Cartier criterion and universal quotient property establish the corrected formula. Over arbitrary characteristic, dual of Sym^n E must not be replaced canonically by Sym^n(E^vee); divided-power issues make the distinction real. Degree0 parametrizes the empty divisor.

statement: Let f:X→S be proper, flat and finitely presented, with universally f*O_X=O_S, and L invertible. If a finitely presented Q corepresents G↦f*(L tensor f*G), the divisors with associated bundle L up to a base twist form a retrocompact open in P(Q). For geometrically integral fibers this is all of P(Q).
computation: Proof: a quotient Q→M corresponds to a section of L tensor f*M. The locus where its restriction to every fiber is regular is open by the flat finite-presentation Cartier criterion; properness of X/S gives the required relative open condition in the parameter. On geometrically integral fibers every nonzero section of an invertible sheaf is regular.
fate: The cohomology corepresentability ingredient is in his own published EGA III2 Th7.7.6, printed69, under a locally noetherian base, proper f and coherent base-flat sheaf;7.7.9(i) gives base change. The relative Cartier and projective-quotient constructions give the open divisor functor. The universal f*O condition is needed for the scalar quotient and uniqueness, and geometric integrality is needed for every nonzero section to be regular. statement: For D⊂X×_S T a relative Cartier family, its fixed-point locus Z consists of x such that the whole fiber T_x lies set-theoretically in D_x. Under universal openness of T/S, Z is closed. If T/S is flat, locally finitely presented with geometrically irreducible S1 fibers, D transposes to a relative Cartier family over X exactly away from Z. With T proper, the analogous associated-point obstruction Z′ is closed.
computation: Proof: X−Z is the image of (X×T)−D under the open projection, hence open. An irreducible noetherian S1 geometric fiber has its unique generic point as its only associated point. A local equation is regular exactly when it avoids that prime, equivalently when it is not nilpotent; mere nonzero is insufficient on a nonreduced fiber. The relative Cartier locus W in X×T is open under the stated finite-presentation and flatness hypotheses. For proper T/S, the image of its closed complement under X×T→X is closed, giving Z′.
fate: The openness and fiberwise Cartier arguments are standard consequences of the relative Cartier criterion. The S1 and geometric irreducibility assumptions cannot be replaced by topological irreducibility alone; regularity is tested at all associated points. The source explicitly distinguishes Z from Z′ in the general case.

statement: A basepoint-free linear system on X/S with projective parameter P corresponds to a morphism to the dual projective bundle whose image on every geometric associated component spans that bundle. This componentwise condition ensures every member is a relative Cartier divisor.
computation: Proof: a section of an invertible sheaf is regular iff it avoids all associated points. A nonzero parameter hyperplane pulls back to zero at an associated generic point precisely when it contains the corresponding component image. Applying this on every geometric fiber gives the assertion.
fate: The universal quotient construction proves the map correspondence; the componentwise spanning condition is exactly nonvanishing at all associated points. The weaker condition that the union of all components spans does not suffice, since a hyperplane may contain one component.

statement: Let X→S be locally of finite presentation, F a quasi-coherent finitely presented S-flat module, T⊂X closed, and j:X−T→X a quasi-compact open immersion. Fiberwise depth of F at every point of T at least1 gives F→j*F|U injective; depth at least2 gives an isomorphism. In the line-bundle application X/S is flat with fiberwise depth of O_X at least2 on T: then a bundle L on U extends invertibly exactly when j*L is invertible, uniquely with its comparison.
computation: Proof: locally a finitely generated ideal defines T because j is quasi-compact. The fiber-depth hypothesis supplies a length1 or2 regular sequence in that ideal after localization; EGA IV3 11.3.8 lifts its regularity for the base-flat module. The local-cohomology sequence0→H^0_T(F)→F→j*F|U→H^1_T(F)→0 then gives injectivity or bijectivity. In the noetherian case this is exactly IV2 5.10.2/5.10.5. Apply the depth2 statement to Hom bundles for uniqueness of invertible extensions; if j*L is invertible it supplies existence.

statement: In the locally factorial setting, a divisor on an open whose complement has codimension at least2 extends uniquely as a Cartier divisor; the associated line bundle extension gives the corresponding rational-map/linear-system extension when the stated nondegeneracy remains true.
computation: Proof: on a locally factorial noetherian scheme a codimension1 cycle defines a Cartier divisor. Closure of the codimension1 components from U gives the unique Weil divisor on X because the complement contributes none. Local factoriality makes this closure Cartier.
fate: The regular-local factoriality theorem and the Cartier–Weil correspondence are classical ingredients. The source does not prove an unrestricted extension across codimension1, and the earlier fixed-divisor ambiguity must not be reintroduced.

statement: The section criterion on scans123–125 twice says every geometric section is regular, omitting the word nonzero. On a nonempty fiber the zero section is a zerodivisor, so the literal statement excludes all systems.

statement: For proper flat geometrically integral fibers and a cohomology corepresentative Q, linear systems with fixed parameter rank correspond to locally free quotients Q→E^vee, modulo parameter isomorphism, hence to a Grassmannian. A system is complete exactly when its fiber spaces equal all H^0(X_s,L_s).
computation: Proof: adjunction identifies a section map E→f*L with a map Q→E^vee; fiberwise injectivity of the former is fiberwise surjectivity of the latter. Nakayama gives a locally free quotient. Completeness means this quotient has full fiber dimension and the cohomology base-change comparison is an isomorphism.
fate: EGA III2 Th7.7.6 supplies Q; the Grassmannian quotient functor gives the moduli statement. Completeness is preserved by base change when stated geometrically with the required cohomology/base-change isomorphisms. A marginal apparent negation in scan126 conflicts with that formulation and is flagged without alteration.

statement: The projective-frame lemma requires each specified component image to span the projective parameter space. Under that hypothesis an automorphism fixing the images is scalar on the associated vector space; merely spanning by the union of components is insufficient.
computation: Proof: n+2 points in projective general position form a projective frame; fixing the first n+1 diagonalizes a representing matrix, and fixing their sum makes all diagonal entries equal. A union of coordinate points spans but admits a diagonal torus of automorphisms, so the weakened union formulation fails.
fate: This is the classical projective-frame argument. It supports the revised automorphism-faithfulness proof, with scheme-valued infinitesimal verification still needed for a monomorphism of functors.

statement: For an effective Cartier D⊂X the tangent space to Div at D is H^0(D,N_D/X); the tangent space to Hom(X,P) at f is Hom(f*Ω_P,O_X). The proof of functorial faithfulness needs Artin-local/infinitesimal control, not only injectivity on geometric points.
computation: Proof: deform an ideal locally generated by t to(t+εa); changing the generator identifies a modulo(t), giving Hom(I/I²,O_D)=N_D/X. A map deformation is a derivation f^*O_P→O_X, equivalently Hom(f*Ω_P,O_X). These are first-order statements only; induction along square-zero extensions is required for the stated stronger functor conclusion.
fate: Grothendieck’s published Bourbaki Exposé221 (May1961),5.3–5.5, printed270–271, explicitly gives the Hilbert tangent and Cartier-divisor formulas. The square-zero calculation also proves the Hom formula. The text’s O_P in that formula is a type error. Its references to future §§25–26 do not establish the general arbitrary-functor monomorphism criterion, which remains a separate incomplete step; the1961 tangent result is already known when this draft is written.

statement: Uniqueness of the parameter identification permits fppf descent of a linear system, but the descended parameter need only be a Brauer–Severi variety. Scan137 proposes treating projective bundles and their twisted forms using PGL torsors.
computation: Proof: choose local identifications with P^(r−1). Their overlaps give a PGL_r cocycle; effective faithfully flat descent yields the twisted projective scheme. Lifting the cocycle to GL_r is exactly the additional obstruction to obtaining the projectivization of a global vector bundle.
fate: This is the standard PGL-torsor/Brauer–Severi correspondence. Reineke–Schröer2017 §2, printed453–454, explicitly recalls the general scheme version and the GL-lift obstruction; only those preliminaries are used. The proposed future exposition is not present in the supplied pages.

statement: Proposition4.4 asks for a proof that, under H^0(X,O_X)=k, the set of k-rational members determines a linear system, and asks for the exact generality over imperfect fields and counterexamples. The hypotheses about regularity and available rational members must be retained.
computation: Proof in the stated restricted case: two sections with the same effective divisor have ratio an everywhere invertible global function, hence an element of k*. Every nonzero vector in a k-vector space defines a k-rational projective point. Equality of their represented lines therefore recovers the subspace. This does not prove the extra imperfect-field/descent assertions.
fate: For the geometrically integral proper setting and actual k-linear section subspaces, equal divisors identify sections up to k* and equality of all projective k-points determines the subspace. statement: On the singular-zero scheme of a line-bundle section, the second principal part is a canonical quadratic form in the relative cotangent module, with the line-bundle twist. Its polar determinant defines a closed nonsupersingularity obstruction compatible with arbitrary base change.
computation: Proof: changing local coordinates changes the quadratic term by the symmetric-square cotangent change when the constant and linear terms vanish. Replacing a local equation by a unit multiplies its quadratic term by that unit. Determinants transform by the square determinant character and the appropriate line-bundle power, so they glue and commute with base change.
fate: The modern quadratic-form treatment in Conrad2014 AppendixC and SGA7II XII gives the determinant construction. This polar determinant detects nonsupersingularity; in odd rank characteristic2 it does not detect ordinary smoothness, which instead uses the half-discriminant.

statement: The proof identifies smoothness of a closed subscheme with injectivity of its conormal map as a sheaf, without specifying fiberwise injectivity or a locally split injection.
computation: Proof: in B=k[x,y]/(xy), the conormal map B→B² sends1 to(y,x). Its kernel is ann(x)∩ann(y)=(y)∩(x)=0, so it is sheaf-injective. At the origin its fiber map is zero, and Spec(B) is a singular node.
fate: For an lci immersion into a smooth scheme the smoothness criterion is injectivity after passage to the residue field, equivalently local splitting with locally free cokernel. A merely injective sheaf map allows singular hypersurfaces.

statement: The isolated nonsupersingular hypersurface claim is correct under regular-local ambient assumptions, but the early normality threshold uses the ambient dimension as if it were the hypersurface dimension. In a regular-local presentation one removes m−1 independent linear equations, leaving a hypersurface whose quadratic initial form is smooth.

statement: Scan154 identifies an invertible direct-summand kernel with a fiber-rank condition; scan166 expressly corrects that earlier equivalence on page15 line10. The separate constant-rank lemma on scan155 already assumes that the exterior-power map vanishes as a morphism, not merely at residue-field points, and is valid with its remaining rank hypothesis. In the later conormal presentation on scan169, local freeness of the cokernel and of the target implies flatness of the image and hence arbitrary kernel base change.
computation: Proof: multiplication by ε on A=k[ε]/(ε²) is zero on its unique residue field but is not the zero map. In contrast, if a rank-r minor is a unit, row/column reduction puts a matrix in block form diag(I_r,B); vanishing of all(r+1)-minors forces B=0 as a matrix over A.
fate: Under vanishing of the next minors and invertibility of one maximal surviving minor, matrix row reduction gives a split constant-rank presentation; then kernel, image and cokernel are locally free and commute with all base change. The nilpotent-base distinction is essential.

statement: A degree-e form on a finite locally free module is smooth if it is nonzero on every fiber and its projective zero scheme is smooth over the base. This is detected after arbitrary surjective base change and defines an open locus. The Jacobian criterion uses the ideal generated by the form and all partial derivatives.
computation: Proof: the nonsmooth locus of the projective hypersurface is closed in a proper parameter-family fiber, so its image is closed. Fiberwise smoothness plus the fiberwise nonzero Cartier condition gives smoothness. On an affine chart the Jacobian ideal is generated by f and its derivatives; homogeneous compatibility gives the irrelevant-ideal power criterion.
fate: The smoothness criterion and properness of projective space give openness. Euler’s formula permits dropping the form only when e is invertible; retaining it makes the statement valid in every characteristic. SGA7II XII supplies the quadratic special case, and the general relative Jacobian criterion is EGA IV.

statement: The finite-separable-residue statement compares absolute and geometric elementary singularities at closed points. The author asks whether finite can be removed. For an arbitrary nonclosed point with separably generated residue field, that strengthening is false.

After K=k(t) base change, the K-rational point t=t0 has local tangent cone K[x,y,w]/(xy), where w=t−t0. Its projective quadric is singular at[0:0:1], and the singular locus is not isolated. fate: Closed finite separable residue extensions do not introduce extra tangent directions, so the standard comparison holds. At a nonclosed point, base change to its residue field followed by the rational geometric point changes the local embedding dimension; the proposed strengthening fails.

statement: For a positive-rank locally free module, a quadratic form is smooth when it is fiberwise nonzero and its projective quadric is smooth. A nondegenerate polar form implies smoothness; the converse holds in even rank or when2 is invertible. In odd rank characteristic2, smoothness instead means polar radical dimension1 and nonzero quadratic restriction to that line.
computation: Proof: over a field a projective singular point is a nonzero vector v with B(v,−)=0 and Q(v)=0. If2 is invertible, B(v,v)=2Q(v) makes any radical vector singular. In characteristic2, an alternating polar matrix has even rank; smoothness permits exactly a one-dimensional radical on which Q is nonzero. These fiber criteria give the statement over a base.

statement: For odd rank, the determinant of the universal polar matrix is divisible over Z by2 with content exactly2. statement: Smooth rank-n quadratic forms are equivalent to fppf torsors under the standard orthogonal group O_n. The equivalence sends a form to its isomorphism torsor and a torsor to the descended standard vector bundle and quadratic form.

statement: The draft asserts étale local triviality in the smooth-orthogonal cases and a Zariski-local finite étale strengthening via SGA3 XXIV; in odd rank it proposes first a finite locally free μ2 cover and then the smooth-group theorem. It supplies the rank-one characteristic2 example obstructing étale trivialization. These paragraphs assert cover results; the nearby priority and terminology question concerns the corrected discriminant and is separately recorded as C-SA23-hyp-106.
computation: Targeted proof check: original and corrected SGA3 XXIV4.1.1 and4.2.3 were read, including the split-torus/Pic(semilocal)=0 argument. The orthogonal component quotient is finite étale in even rank and when2 is invertible; the connected split SO factor is reductive. In odd rank O=μ2×SO′, so first take the finite locally free μ2 torsor and then the finite étale SO′ cover of the resulting semilocal ring. For a∈k* nonsquare in characteristic2, an isometry aT²≅T² needs a purely inseparable square root, which no separable extension contains; k[t]/(t²−a) is nevertheless a finite faithfully flat cover.
fate: SGA3 XXIV4.2.3 proves that a torsor under a split reductive group over a semilocal base is trivialized by a finite étale surjective cover. Apply this to the split special orthogonal factor after the finite component torsor; in odd rank first use the finite locally free μ2 torsor. Finite presentation spreads the resulting cover and isometry from a local base to a Zariski neighborhood. Thus the asserted Zariski-local finite étale trivialization in the smooth cases, and finite flat trivialization in general, are established. This is not a theorem about arbitrary smooth groups.

statement: The author asks whether, after a degree-n Veronese with n≥2, the dual discriminant can no longer contain the family of all hyperplanes through a fixed positive-dimensional linear subspace C. No transversality or first-jet hypothesis on C is written. The unrestricted hope is false even for the degree2 embedding of a smooth projective plane in characteristic0.
computation: computations.py veronese_fixed_linear_space verifies q(p)=0 and all three partial derivatives vanish at p=[0:0:1] for q=a x²+b y². Proof: take k algebraically closed of characteristic0, f=id on P², and its degree2 Veronese v₂:P²→P⁵. The independent coordinate equations U_x²=U_y²=0 define C≅P³. Every hyperplane containing C pulls back to a nonzero member of that pencil, which is singular at p. The intersection C∩v₂(P²) has local ideal(x²,y²), so it is even finite, although nonreduced. For every degree n≥2 the analogous pencil a x^n+b y^n lies in the square of the maximal ideal at p and gives the same obstruction. All smoothness, irreducibility, projectivity and unramifiedness assumptions on X and f hold.
fate: The unrestricted question has a negative answer by the explicit pencil a x²+b y² constructed here. Stacks33.47.1 and33.47.3 distinguish smoothness away from a fixed base subscheme from the first-jet obstruction at its points. Wutz2016 Theorem1.2 gives a finite-field analogue with embedding-dimension restrictions, not an unrestricted fixed-linear-space theorem. No historical priority is claimed for this counterexample.

statement: For a flat, locally finitely presented projective morphism X→S, the source promises a later proof that the functor of relative effective Cartier divisors on X is representable. This general functor is distinct from fixing the associated line bundle L and from the special projective-bundle formula.
computation: Targeted proof check: the opened original section4, printed150–152, explains the relative Cartier condition, arbitrary base change and the open immersion into Hilb, then invokes Hilbert-scheme existence. For a Hilbert family D⊂X_T, the non-Cartier locus is closed in the proper X_T; removing its image from T gives the required open parameter locus. The finite-presentation extension descends a projective flat model and the finite presentation of D to noetherian approximations; it is a modern extension, not a hypothesis silently attributed to the printed1962 proposition.
fate: Grothendieck’s Bourbaki232 Proposition4.1 (1962), printed152, is the exact projective-flat representability statement over a locally noetherian base: Div is an open subfunctor of Hilb. The arbitrary-base finite-presentation version uses noetherian approximation in addition. The deleted manuscript promise has no independently established date relative to this publication; classA records its own-publication counterpart without a claim of historical priority.
